questions.question: What are design patterns and why do they exist? They are reusable, named solutions to recurring design problems — shared vocabulary that lets a team say 'use a Strategy here' instead of re-deriving the design.
questions.title: Design Patterns Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Design patterns are reusable, named solutions to common problems in object-oriented design — proven arrangements of classes and objects that resolve a recurring force (creating objects, decoupling behavior, varying algorithms). They exist so a team can communicate design at a higher level ('use a Factory here', 'this is a Strategy') instead of re-deriving each solution from first principles, and so that proven, reviewed structures are preferred over ad-hoc ones that look fine but fail under extension.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand patterns as named, force-driven solutions to recurring design problems — and can name the force each resolves and when NOT to apply it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing the 23 GoF patterns and applying them everywhere ('I'll use a Singleton') without naming the force the pattern resolves or the cost it adds.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Group patterns by intent — creational (how to make objects), structural (how to compose them), behavioral (how to assign responsibility) — and for each, name the force it resolves and the cost it adds, so you can also say when NOT to apply it.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Design patterns are reusable, named solutions to recurring problems in software design — the result of recognizing that certain arrangements of classes and objects solve a force (object creation, behavior variation, component composition) repeatedly, and that naming them gives a team shared vocabulary. They exist because re-deriving a good design for a common problem every time is slow and inconsistent: a pattern like Strategy or Observer captures a proven structure so a team can say 'use a Factory here' and everyone understands the intent, the structure, and the trade-off without a long explanation.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) patterns are categorized by intent — creational (how objects are made: Singleton, Factory, Builder), structural (how classes are composed: Adapter, Decorator, Facade), behavioral (responsibility assignment: Strategy, Observer, Command); (2) every pattern resolves a force and adds a cost — a Singleton adds global state, a Decorator adds layers, an Observer adds coupling to update order; (3) the Gang of Four catalog is the classic 23, but patterns also live in concurrency, enterprise, and architecture; (4) SOLID principles are the axioms patterns implement — Strategy implements Open/Closed, Dependency Injection implements Dependency Inversion; (5) patterns are a vocabulary more than a prescription; (6) over-applying patterns is the most common misuse.

sections.title: Strategy pattern — vary behavior without changing the client
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is abstraction versus accidental complexity: a pattern adds indirection that pays off only when the force it resolves is real; applying it to a non-recurring problem adds layers that make code harder, not easier, to change. A second tension: patterns implement SOLID principles but can also obscure them — a deeply nested Decorator chain can violate simplicity even as it satisfies Open/Closed. The third: the shared vocabulary is the real win, so a team must agree on the names — using 'Factory' for a static factory method, 'Builder' for a fluent setter, or 'Repository' for a DAO that isn't a pattern muddies communication.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Patterns are reusable named solutions to recurring design problems — the value is the shared vocabulary and the proven structure.
They group by intent: creational (making objects), structural (composing them), behavioral (assigning responsibility).
Every pattern resolves a force and adds a cost — a Singleton adds global state, a Decorator adds layers — so always ask what it costs.
SOLID is the axioms; patterns are the instances — Strategy realizes Open/Closed, DI realizes Dependency Inversion.
Over-applying patterns is the most common misuse: apply a pattern when the force is real, not because the pattern is famous.
The vocabulary only works if the team agrees on the names — mislabeling a static factory as a 'Factory' or a DAO as a 'Repository' muddies communication.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Design patterns are reusable, named solutions to recurring problems in software design, and they exist so a team can communicate at a higher level — 'use a Strategy here' — instead of re-deriving the design every time. I group them by intent: creational for how objects are made, structural for how they're composed, and behavioral for who has responsibility. The thing I always stress is that every pattern resolves a specific force and adds a cost — a Singleton buys a single instance but adds global state, a Decorator buys composable behavior but adds layers — so the decision is whether the force is real enough to justify the cost. And underneath them are the SOLID principles; Strategy is Open/Closed in action, dependency injection is Dependency Inversion in action. The most common mistake I see is over-applying patterns just because they're famous, which adds indirection that makes code harder, not easier, to change.

followup_questions: When does the Strategy pattern justify its cost over a single method with a switch statement?
How does the Decorator pattern realize the Open/Closed principle, and when does it violate simplicity?
Why is a Singleton often an anti-pattern, and what's the modern alternative for a single instance?
How do SOLID principles and design patterns relate — which principle does each pattern implement?

questions.question: Explain the SOLID principles with Java examples. When would you intentionally violate one?
questions.title: SOLID Principles in Java — Practical Application and Trade-offs
questions.direct_answer: SOLID is five object-oriented design principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. They guide class design toward maintainability and extensibility. However, applying them dogmatically leads to over-engineering — the skill is knowing when each one earns its complexity cost.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of OOP design principles beyond definitions — practical application and trade-off awareness
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting definitions without concrete examples, or treating SOLID as absolute rules rather than guidelines with costs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show when you would intentionally violate a principle (e.g., SRP vs simple CRUD) and explain the cost-benefit

sections.title: The Maintenance Tax Nobody Budgets For
sections.content:
Most codebases don't collapse under the weight of bad algorithms — they collapse under the weight of **bad coupling**. A developer changes the email provider, and three unrelated tests break. Someone adds a discount type, and the checkout method swells by another 20 lines. A new team member extends a class, and the subtype silently violates its parent's contract.

SOLID principles are Robert C. Martin's response to these specific failure modes. They're five concrete rules that prevent the most common ways classes become painful to change. Each one targets a specific kind of coupling that makes modifications expensive.

But here's what most explanations miss: **every SOLID principle adds indirection**. More interfaces, more classes, more files to navigate. For a 200-line CRUD microservice, full SOLID compliance creates 15 files where 3 would suffice. The real engineering skill isn't memorizing the five letters — it's knowing **when each principle earns its abstraction cost** and when YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) is the better call. Interviewers test exactly this: can you apply the principles AND articulate when you'd consciously break them?

sections.title: S — Why 'One Reason to Change' Is Not About Method Count
O — Extending Behavior Without Reopening Tested Code
L — The Subtype That Promises One Thing and Does Another
I — Fat Interfaces Force Implementors to Lie
D — The Principle Spring Was Built On
SOLID at a Glance — Principle, Benefit, and When to Break It
sections.content:
| Principle | One-line Rule | Practical Benefit | When to Violate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S** — SRP | One axis of change per class | Email provider change can't break registration | Tiny microservice where splitting adds navigation cost |
| **O** — OCP | Extend, don't modify | New discount type = new class, zero edits | Only 2 cases with no plans for more |
| **L** — LSP | Subtypes honor parent contract | No runtime UnsupportedOperationException surprises | JDK's unmodifiableList — pragmatic JDK trade-off |
| **I** — ISP | Small, focused interfaces | No forced no-op method stubs | Simple CRUD controller with 4 methods |
| **D** — DIP | Depend on abstractions | Swap DB, inject mock — zero service changes | Scripts, prototypes, performance-critical inner loops |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SRP is about stakeholders, not method count** — a class with 10 methods serving one business concern is fine; a class with 3 methods serving 3 different change sources is a violation
- **OCP via Spring component scanning** — new `@Component` strategies are discovered automatically at startup, so extending behavior requires zero edits to the consuming code
- **LSP violations surface as runtime UnsupportedOperationException** — prefer composition over inheritance so contract mismatches fail at compile time, not in production
- **Spring Data's repository hierarchy is textbook ISP** — `CrudRepository` for basic CRUD, `JpaRepository` for JPA-specific features; depend on the smallest interface that covers your needs
- **DIP via constructor injection is nearly free** — the only SOLID principle where the cost of following it is lower than the cost of violating it
- **SOLID is a cost-benefit analysis** — the interview-winning answer explains WHEN the abstraction pays for itself, not just WHAT each letter means

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
SOLID gives you five rules for structuring classes so changes don't ripple unpredictably through your codebase. **Single Responsibility** means one axis of change per class — if your `UserService` handles registration, emails, and reports, changing the email provider risks breaking registration logic. Extract separate services.

**Open/Closed** is about extending behavior without modifying existing code. In Spring, the Strategy pattern with `@Component` scanning is the natural implementation — add a new `DiscountStrategy` class and the consuming service discovers it automatically, no edits needed.

**Liskov Substitution** catches subtype lies. If `ReadOnlyList` extends `ArrayList` but throws on `add()`, any code expecting a `List` breaks at runtime. The fix is composition — expose only the methods the wrapper actually supports, so the mismatch becomes a compile error.

**Interface Segregation** keeps interfaces small. Spring Data does this well — `CrudRepository` for basic CRUD, `JpaRepository` for JPA-specific operations. Extend only what you need so implementations don't carry dead methods.

**Dependency Inversion** is Spring's foundation. Depend on `OrderRepository` the interface, inject the concrete implementation via constructor. Testing injects a mock, production injects JPA — the service doesn't know the difference.

The nuance that separates a good answer from a great one is knowing **when to break these rules**. A 200-line microservice doesn't need five single-responsibility classes — the navigation cost outweighs the coupling cost. My rule: follow SOLID when the abstraction earns its weight, violate it consciously when simplicity wins. DIP through constructor injection is the one I never skip — the cost is essentially zero.
